source_text: ἐξ εὐωνύμων. Καὶ ἐπηρώτησα, καὶ εἶπα πρὸς τὸν ἄγγελον τὸν λαλοῦντα ἐν ἐμοὶ, λέγων, Κύριε, τί ἐστι ταῦτα; καὶ εἶπε πρὸς μὲ, λέγων, Οὐ γινώσκεις τί ἐστι ταῦτα; Καὶ εἶπα, Οὐχὶ, Κύριε.» Ὁ μὲν οὖν μακάριος προφήτης διεπυνθάνετο λέγων, Τί ἐστι ταῦτα, Κύριε; Βραχὺ δὲ διήγημα παρενθεὶς ὁ θεσπέσιος ἄγγελος διερμηνεύει τὴν ὅρασιν, καὶ τὴν τῆς λυχνίας κατασκευὴν εἰς Χριστὸν ἀναφέρει λέγων περὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ λύχνων ἑπτὰ, «Οὗτοι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ Κυρίου, ἐπιβλέποντες ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν.» Εἰ γὰρ χρή τι καὶ τῶν παχυτέρων εἰπεῖν, μυρίοις ὅσοις ἡμᾶς ὀφθαλμοῖς τὸ θεῖον ὁρᾷ καὶ κατασκέπτεται τὰ ἀνθρώπινα, γινώσκων τὰ ἐν τῷ σκότει, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, «Καὶ τὸ φῶς μετ' αὐτοῦ ἐστιν.» Εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἡμῖν τοῖς ἐν κόσμῳ τὸ φῶς ἐνίησι Θεὸς, καταπλουτήσειεν ἂν αὐτὸ καὶ πρό γε τῶν ἄλλων ἐν ἰδίᾳ φύσει λαχών. Ἢ εἴπερ οὐχ ὧδε ἔχειν ὑποπτεύουσί τινες, ὥρα που τάχα τοῖς ὧδε φρονεῖν ἑλομένοις ἐπιφωνεῖν, «Σύνετε δὴ ἄφρονες ἐν τῷ λαῷ, καὶ μωροί ποτε φρονήσατε. Ὁ φυτεύσας τὸ οὖς, οὐχὶ ἀκούει; ἢ ὁ πλάσας τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν, οὐχὶ κατανοεῖ; Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἐνεργὴς, καὶ ἠκονημένος μᾶλλον μαχαίρας διστόμου, διικνούμενος μέχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος, ἁρμῶν τε καὶ μυελῶν, καὶ κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ. Πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ.» Φωτίζει δὴ οὖν καὶ ἐφορᾷ πάντα Χριστός. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ ἔφασκε δι' ἑνὸς τῶν προφητῶν· «Θεὸς ἐγγίζων ἐγώ εἰμι, λέγει Κύριος, καὶ οὐχὶ Θεὸς πόῤῥωθεν. Μὴ ἀπ' ἐμοῦ κρυβήσεταί τι;» Λάθοι γὰρ ἂν οὐδὲν τὸν πάντα εἰδότα νοῦν. Ἢ οὐκ ἄριστά σοι ταῦτα διεσκέφθαι δοκῶ; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Παντάπασι μὲν οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἀσύνηθες δέ τι περὶ τὴν λυχνίαν ὁ προφήτης ὁρῶν, ἐλαιῶν γὰρ ἦσαν κλάδοι, προσεπυνθάνετο λέγων, «Τί αἱ δύο ἐλαῖαι αὗται αἱ ἐκ δεξιῶν τῆς λυχνίας καὶ ἐξ εὐωνύμων; Καὶ ἐπηρώτησα,» φησὶν, «ἐκ δευτέρου, καὶ εἶπα πρὸς αὐτόν· Τί οἱ δύο κλάδοι τῶν ἐλαιῶν, οἱ ἐν ταῖς χερσὶ τῶν δύο μυξωτήρων τῶν χρυσῶν, τῶν ἐπιχεόντων καὶ ἐπαναγόντων τὰς ἐπαρυστρίδας τὰς χρυσᾶς; Καὶ εἶπε πρός με,» φησὶν, «Οὐ γινώσκεις τί ἐστι ταῦτα; Καὶ εἶπα, Οὐχὶ, Κύριε. Καὶ εἶπέ μοι· Οὗτοι οἱ δύο υἱοὶ τῆς πιότητος παρεστήκασι τῷ Κυρίῳ πάσης τῆς γῆς.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Τίς οὖν ἄρα γέγονε χρεία τῷ μακαρίῳ προφήτῃ, τοῦ καὶ εἰς αὖθις ἀναπυθέσθαι δεῖν; Ἐπηρώτησα γὰρ, φησὶν, ἐκ δευτέρου. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ φαίης ἂν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, σοφόν τε εἶναι καὶ πρέπον, τοῖς γε ὅλως ὀρθὰ φρονεῖν ᾑρημένοις, ἀκριβεῖς καὶ ἀπεξεσμένους τὰς ἐφ' ὅτῳ οὖν τῶν ἀναγκαίων ποιεῖσθαι πεύσεις; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Φημί. {ΚΥΡ.} Κλῶνας δὴ οὖν ἐλαιῶν θαλῷ βρύοντας ἁπαλῷ καὶ νεοθαλεῖ τεθεαμένος ὁ προφήτης, ἐλαίας αὐτοὺς, καὶ οὐκ ἐξ ἐλαιῶν ὠνόμαζε κλάδους. Εἶτα σεσιώπηκεν ὁ θεσπέσιος ἄγγελος, τὴν ἐμφρονεστέραν καὶ
pass_a_gloss: [End of Zechariah quotation from s.11] ...and one from the left (ex euōnymōn). And I asked (epērōtēsa) and said to the angel speaking in me (ho lalōn en emoi), saying: Lord, what are these? He said: Do you not know what these are? I said: No, lord. | So the blessed prophet inquired (diepynthaneto): What are these, Lord? The divine (thespesios) angel, having inserted (parentheis) a short narrative (diēgēma), interprets (diermēneuei) the vision (horasis) and refers (anapherei) the construction (kataskeuē) of the lampstand (lychnia) to Christ, saying of the seven lamps (lychnoi) on it: These are the eyes of the Lord, looking upon (epiblepontes) all the earth. | For if one must say something of the cruder kind (tōn pachyterōn), the divine (to theion) sees us with countless (myriois hosois) eyes and surveys (kataskeptetai) human things, knowing the things in darkness (skotos), as written: 'And the light is with him.' | For if God puts light into (eniēsi) us in the world, he would abound in it (kataploutēseien) himself, having obtained (lachōn) it in his own nature (idia physei) before the others. | Or if some suspect (hypopteuousi) it is not so, it is perhaps time to cry out (epiphōnein) to those choosing to think so: [Ps 93:8-9 LXX] Understand (synete), senseless ones (aphrones) among the people, and fools (mōroi), at some time be wise (pote phronēsate). He who planted (phyteusas) the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed (plasas) the eye, does he not perceive (katanoei)? [Heb 4:12-13] For living (zōn) the word of God, and active (energēs), and sharpened (ēkonēmenos) more than a two-mouthed sword (machaira distomos), passing through (diiknoumenos) to division (merismos) of soul and spirit, joints (harmoi) and marrows (myeloi), and judging (kritikos) thoughts (enthymēseis) and notions (ennoiai) of heart; no creature (ktisis) unseen (aphanēs) before him; all naked (gymna) and laid bare (tetrachēlismena) to his eyes. | So Christ illumines (phōtizei) and oversees (ephora) all. Therefore he said through one of the prophets: I am a God drawing near (engizōn), says the Lord, and not a God from afar (porrōthen). Will anything be hidden (krybēsetai) from me? For nothing could escape (lathoi) the mind (nous) that knows all. Or do I not seem to you to have examined (dieskephthai) these things excellently? | PALL.: Altogether so. | CYR.: Seeing something unaccustomed (asynēthes) about the lampstand (for there were branches of olives, kladoi elaiōn), the prophet inquired further (prosepynthaneto): [Zech 4:11-14] What are these two olives (elaiai) on the right and left of the lampstand? And I asked a second time (ek deuterou): What are the two branches of the olives that are in the hands of (en tais chersi, i.e. beside) the two golden nozzles (myxōtēres), pouring on (epicheontōn) and bringing up (epanagontōn) the golden oil-funnels (eparystrides)? He said: Do you not know? I: No, lord. He: These are the two sons of fatness (hyioi tēs piotētos); they stand by (parestēkasi) the Lord of all the earth. | PALL.: What need then did the blessed prophet have to inquire again (anapythesthai)? For he says: I asked a second time. | CYR.: Would you not say, Palladius, that it is wise and fitting (prepon) for those who have chosen to think rightly entirely, to make exact (akribeis) and polished (apexesmenous) inquiries (peuseis) about any of the necessary things? | PALL.: I say so. | CYR.: The prophet, having beheld olive sprigs (klōnes) teeming (bryontas) with tender (hapalos) new-blooming (neothalēs) foliage (thallos), named them olives, and not branches from olives. Then the divine angel was silent (sesiōpēken), awaiting (perimenōn) the more sensible (emphronesteran) and [continues in s.13]

pass_b_english: Cyril: …and one on the left.” And I asked and said to the angel who spoke in me, “My lord, what are these?” And he said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.”’ (Zechariah 4:3–5) So the blessed prophet asked, ‘What are these, my lord?’ And the divine angel, after inserting a short account (Zechariah 4:6–10), interprets the vision and refers the making of the lampstand to Christ, saying of the seven lamps on it, ‘These are the eyes of the Lord, which look upon the whole earth.’ (Zechariah 4:10) For if we must say something in rather bodily terms, the Godhead sees us with countless eyes and surveys human affairs, ‘knowing what is in the darkness,’ as it is written, ‘and the light is with him’ (Daniel 2:22). For if God puts light even into us who are in the world, he would surely be rich in it himself, since he has it in his own nature before all others. Or if some suspect that this is not so, it is perhaps time to cry out to those who have chosen to think that way: ‘Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, be wise at last. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?’ (Psalm 94:8–9) ‘For the word of God is living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes.’ (Hebrews 4:12–13) Christ, then, gives light to all things and watches over all things. That is why he also said through one of the prophets: ‘I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24) For nothing could escape the mind that knows all things. Or do I not seem to you to have examined this very well?

Cyril: But the prophet saw something unusual about the lampstand, for olive branches were there, and so he asked further: ‘What are these two olive trees on the right of the lampstand and on the left? And I asked a second time,’ he says, ‘and said to him, “What are the two branches of the olive trees that are beside the two golden spouts, which pour out and draw up the golden oil vessels?” And he said to me,’ he says, ‘“Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, my lord.” And he said to me, “These are the two sons of richness, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.”’ (Zechariah 4:11–14)
Palladius: Then what need did the blessed prophet have to ask yet again? For he says, ‘I asked a second time’ (Zechariah 4:12).

Cyril: Would you not say, Palladius, that it is wise and fitting for those who have chosen to think rightly in every respect to make their inquiries about any necessary matter precise and carefully refined?

Cyril: Well then: when the prophet saw olive shoots teeming with tender, fresh leaves, he called them olive trees, and not branches from olive trees. Then the divine angel kept silent, waiting for a more thoughtful and…

choices.why: LXX 'sons of fatness' (υἱοὶ τῆς πιότητος; Hebrew 'sons of oil', the anointed ones) is rendered 'sons of richness' to keep the oil image Cyril uses in s.13.
ἐν ταῖς χερσί ('in the hands of') rendered 'beside', as the LXX idiom means; μυξωτῆρες = spouts (nozzles of the lamps); ἐπαρυστρίδες = oil vessels (lamp funnels).
Κύριε addressed to the angel is rendered 'my lord', lowercase, since it does not mean God; 'the Lord of all the earth' stays capitalised.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril De adoratione Book 9 exists. Translated fresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the earlier English of this book was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

Section opens mid-quotation: the Zechariah quotation began in s.11 at Zechariah 4:1; the part in this section is 4:3b–5, so the inline citation names only 4:3–5. 'A short account' is the word to Zerubbabel, Zechariah 4:6–10a, which Cyril skips; cited because the reference is unambiguous. 'These are the eyes of the Lord' is Zechariah 4:10b LXX (LXX adds 'seven'; Cyril omits it). Daniel 2:22 follows the Theodotion Greek. Psalm 93:8–9 LXX = Psalm 94:8–9 English. Cyril runs Hebrews 4:12–13 straight on from the Psalm inside one quotation; split into two citations. His Hebrews wording differs from the standard NT text ('sharpened more than a two-edged sword' for 'sharper than any two-edged sword'; 'judging thoughts and notions of the heart'); rendered as he quotes it. 'Shall anything be hidden from me?' is Cyril's loose wording of Jeremiah 23:24 LXX ('If anyone hides in secret places, shall I not see him?'); cited as 23:23–24. 'Christ gives light to all' may echo John 1:9; left uncited as doubtful. LXX 'sons of fatness' (υἱοὶ τῆς πιότητος; Hebrew 'sons of oil', the anointed ones) is rendered 'sons of richness' to keep the oil image Cyril uses in s.13. ἐν ταῖς χερσί ('in the hands of') rendered 'beside', as the LXX idiom means; μυξωτῆρες = spouts (nozzles of the lamps); ἐπαρυστρίδες = oil vessels (lamp funnels). The section ends mid-phrase at the PG column break; the sentence completes in s.13. Κύριε addressed to the angel is rendered 'my lord', lowercase, since it does not mean God; 'the Lord of all the earth' stays capitalised.

changes: Vocative Κύριε to the angel: 'Lord' -> 'my lord' (three places; the angel is not God)
'he answered me' -> 'he said to me' (εἶπε πρὸς μέ)
Added 'also' for τοιγάρτοι καί before Jeremiah 23:23–24
Row 2 opening recast into natural English word order, γάρ kept
